newsitem.title: UK: London precious metals forecast to re-test upside.
newsitem.headline: London precious metals forecast to re-test upside.

text.p: The precious metals markets were forecast to try another move higher on Thursday although dealers admitted that bigger prices would attract heavy selling.
"It got capped at around $384.50 on Wednesday and we could see it try that area again today," one dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $382.65 per ounce after $383.60 on Wednesday when the market closed at $383.80/$384.30.
Dealers said spot business was fairly modest so far and largely limited to trades between the professional dealers.
Light selling had taken gold off its European opening level at just over $383.00.

Most of the impetus for this week's firmer tone was coming from the hugely cash rich and mainly U.S-run hedge funds which had decided that the gold price was not going to fall from the $377-$379 level it had occupied since the end of October.
The funds switching position to take advantage of a price rise rather than price fall sparked fresh buying in the market lifting prices from around $378 at the end of last week.
Also helping gold was a weaker dollar against the yen which had shaded some lustre off booming U.S. equity and bond markets.
"I think the potential is there (for gold) but it all depends on the funds," one dealer in continental Europe said.

Dealers said they thought around $382.00 would be about the bottom of the current price cycle but gold producers were expected to take advantage of any rise over $384 by selling metal into the market.
"They are quite happy to wait for a couple of extra dollars before they sell," one dealer said, adding that a rise to over $385 was needed to attract new investors to gold.
"If it were to turn lower now, it would be very disappointing," a dealer said.
Silver prices were also a little off Wedneaday's highs of $4.95 at $4.89/$4.91, down two cents from the close.
"The pivotal number for silver is $4.92. if it can pass that, it could reach $5.00," a dealer said.
However he added that interest in silver was relatively muted and any re-newed buying would be more reflect more of a followthrough to firmer gold than inherent faith in silver.

Palladium was fixed at $120.50, its highest fix since October 4, 1996 reflecting forecasts by leading refiner Johnson Matthey this week that palladium supply would be in a 130,000-ounce deficit this year after a surplus in 1995.
Its sister metal platinum was a little easer at $386.00/$387.00. --Brian Spoors +44 171 542 8058
